015.text: Morgan was telling me the other day...
she said something about the nod. The nod people do in meetings when someone quotes a business book. And I haven't been able to stop noticing it since.

019.text: So here's what happened to me. My manager...
nice guy, genuinely trying to help... he handed me four books in two years.
Good to Great, Lean Startup, Atomic Habits, and one about radical candor.
Four books. Well, three and a half...
I think one was a podcast recommendation that turned into a book.

026.text: We bought Good to Great in bulk.
I had been in consulting maybe three years, and someone above me decided it was going to be our framework.
Every new analyst got a copy. Clients got copies. We quoted it in decks.

028.text: Like a franchise manual. And here's the thing...
it worked. I watched junior consultants read it and come back sharper. They had language for things. Level 5 Leadership. The Hedgehog Concept.
They had a way to think about strategy, not just talk about it.
And some of them... some of them genuinely got better at their jobs.

031.text: The problem came later. Jim Collins held up these companies as exemplars. The companies you should study. Circuit City. Fannie Mae.
Published in two thousand and... oh-one, I think? Doesn't matter.
Within a decade, both had collapsed.

033.text: Both. Circuit City went bankrupt in two thousand and eight.
Fannie Mae collapsed the same year... different cause, but same result.
You remember what happened with Fannie Mae.

034.text: And nobody told me to go check. Those books were already on the shelf when I showed up.
My manager quoted them like they were...
I don't know, settled? Like settled law.
I had no idea the examples underneath had collapsed. You just... trust the shelf.

037.text: That's the thing though. Nobody checks. The book doesn't update.
It's not even about Collins getting it wrong...
the whole genre has no correction mechanism. The book on your shelf doesn't tell you what happened next.

038.text: right, but if we're being honest about it, I kept recommending it. Even after.
Because the frameworks still gave people a way to think about strategy. The case studies were wrong, but the mental models worked.
Or... not worked. I don't know if worked is the right word. They were useful.

046.text: What about you? Morgan's got fifteen years of this.
But you're... what, three years in?

overrides.048: Two and a half. I'm the person these books are written for.

050.text: Okay. My boss kept scheduling me for all-hands presentations. Quarterly numbers, take questions, walk the room. And I kept dreading it.
One weekend I'm in the airport and I see Quiet. Susan Cain. The Power of Introverts in a World That Can't Stop Talking.
I pick it up and I feel...

055.text: I didn't know it had a name.
I just knew that I bought that book because I needed someone with a credential...
a researcher, a TED talk, something bigger than me...
to tell me it was okay to be the person who prepares instead of performs.

057.text: My Mondays changed. I stopped dreading the presentations.
Not because I got better at them.
Because I stopped thinking there was something wrong with me for hating them.
That was real. That actually happened to me.

059.text: ...was a hook on the cover, a credential on the jacket, an enemy called the extrovert ideal, a...
I know what it was doing. I figured that out later.
Doesn't change the fact that my Mondays got better.

063.text: Can I say something? I'm sitting here listening to both of you and I'm...
okay this might be obvious, but it's the same shape. Completely different books but something underneath is...

065.text: My manager hands me Atomic Habits. And the title does this thing where it...
And then I check the back and the guy's got all these...
and then there's a villain, the old way of doing things, and then a system, and then a promise that I'll become...
I bought in. I didn't evaluate anything. The shape just felt right.

069.text: think about what we just did.
Morgan tells a story that... you're hooked, right? She's got the credentials, she's been in the rooms.
There's a villain... the books that don't update.
And then I come in and... I basically gave you the permission chapter.
And Alex just had his transformation moment.
We just... we just did the whole thing. While talking about it.

overrides.072: But that's not the same thing... we're not selling anything.

074.text: I don't know. I genuinely don't know.
I was just telling you what happened to me.
But I think... maybe part of this formula is just the shape of how people tell stories about change.
Any story about I learned something probably has a hook, a turning point.

076.text: the formula is self-aware. It uses every pattern it exposes.
And then it asks whether that makes it more honest... or more sophisticated manipulation.

080.text: I had a guy on my team...
smart, actually probably the sharpest analyst I've worked with, he ended up at...
He figured out the formula before anyone else.
And then he stopped reading anything. Stopped taking frameworks seriously. Stopped learning.
He could see through everything and it made him useless.

overrides.081: The smug version of the nod.

083.text: You refuse to nod because you're above it?

084.text: Where you see the formula and it still works on you.

085.text: My manager gave me those books because he genuinely wanted to help me.
And the books followed a formula that's designed to make me feel changed whether or not I actually change.
